rationale: This overview compares diagnostic patterns, epidemiology and clinical features across several neurodegenerative disorders. Recurrent visual hallucinations inform the description of Lewy body dementia. The review includes no dried fig intake comparison or food-timed visual event measure.

The authors examine potentially treatment-associated impulse-control disorders across clinical settings. The apomorphine discussion concerns prescribed drug exposure and motor or behavioral outcomes. The paper does not pair dried fig consumption with visual hallucination frequency.

The review discusses an oligodendroglial synucleinopathy and distinguishes multiple system atrophy from other parkinsonian syndromes. Its clinical and pathological features provide differential-diagnosis context without a dated dried fig exposure or Parkinson visual event count.

Forty Swedish nursing homes contributed clinical sign and dispensing data. The groups included 440 residents with recorded dementia and 154 without it. The clinical instrument asks about observable visual hallucinations among multiple Lewy body signs. The analysis compares medication use and signs, with no change in visual event frequency after an ingredient.

The authors describe clinical presentation, diagnostic investigations and timing in Slovenian cases identified in 2015. Perceptual symptoms appear in this different disease context. The data do not include a comparison of dried fig intake in Parkinson disease.

This review synthesizes clinical apomorphine studies and describes mixed neuropsychiatric observations. References 182–184 lead to earlier treatment reports. The cited observations use a prescribed drug and may reflect changes to other dopaminergic medications. The review supplies no dried fig comparison or original counted visual outcome.

Clinical histories with inherited OPA1-associated optic atrophy and parkinsonism accompany experiments on mitochondrial pathways in derived cells. The clinical medication and model findings do not measure visual episodes after figs.

Of 338 screened older surgical patients, 104 entered the analysis. The clinical question concerns preoperative nonmotor features and postoperative delirium. The mention of visual hallucinations describes a feature of several distinct syndromes. The paper gives no dried fig intake comparison or separately counted visual episodes.

The investigators map molecular and elemental distributions within human V1 tissue using two mass-spectrometry imaging modalities. These maps concern tissue composition and cortical layers, without a defined population with food exposure and subsequent visual episodes.

Seventy-five people with mild cognitive impairment included 33 with probable Lewy body disease, 15 with possible Lewy body disease and 27 with Alzheimer disease. Clinical features inform the diagnostic grouping. The original compares dopamine-transporter imaging against clinical assessments rather than measuring benefit or harm after a food.

The analysis examined nine Parkinson autopsies, four incidental Lewy body cases and six controls for retinal phosphorylated alpha-synuclein. The comparisons concern postmortem biomarker localization. No culinary exposure or visual episode response was measured.

The authors use brain-bank cases to compare Alzheimer disease with different distributions of Lewy pathology. Onset of clinical features is compared across pathology categories. This supplies diagnostic context without a dried fig exposure or post-ingestion visual episode rate.

Fourteen Parkinson participants with sleep dysfunction, fourteen without it and twelve healthy controls underwent a serotonin-transporter imaging comparison. Binding and sleep status are the endpoints. The study does not measure visual hallucination frequency after food.

The study examines hybrid interpretation scores for ioflupane imaging. Its outcomes concern diagnostic classification and reader measures. Clinical diagnostic references do not provide a dried fig comparison.

The investigators relate regional expression of selected genes to Parkinson brain atrophy patterns. The analysis concerns spatial relationships and neuropathological hypotheses. Food intake and visual event frequency are outside the measured contrast.

The article evaluates whether brain connectivity measures help characterize neurodegenerative disorders. The clinical and imaging groups supply diagnostic context. They do not establish a culinary exposure or change in visual episode frequency.

The authors retrospectively collected drawing measures for 103 people with probable dementia with Lewy bodies. Prognosis was compared by scores on pentagon and clock drawing. The assessments do not provide a controlled food exposure or repeated visual event outcome.

The original classifies visual hallucinations as well-formed and recurrent visual images for clinical characterization. Perfusion and PET comparisons are the measured contrasts. The occurrence criterion differs from an episode rate measured after dried fig intake.

Clinical apathy measures and neuroimaging are compared in Parkinson disease. The outcome is motivation-related phenotype and associated brain changes. The study does not measure a dried fig exposure and visual hallucination frequency response.

The clinical report evaluated recognition of six facial expressions in 107 older patients with Lewy body disease. It examines perceptual task accuracy and describes visual features in the cohort. Task accuracy differs from a timed hallucination count following food intake.
The article considers strategies for neurologic disease affecting auditory pathways and otologic function. It does not test dried figs or clinical Parkinson visual hallucination frequency.

The study recruited 68 people spanning Parkinson disease with dementia, Parkinson disease without dementia and controls. Susceptibility imaging and neuropsychiatric classifications are the study variables. The clinical psychosis and cited visual symptom findings are separate from a food-linked episode rate.

This review describes an inherited progressive myoclonus epilepsy, its molecular pathology and investigational treatments. It does not study a Parkinson dried fig exposure or count visual episodes after ingestion.

The IDEAL study compares dementia subtypes on quality of life, wellbeing and satisfaction measures. Symptoms and diagnoses characterize the study participants. These cross-sectional measures are not visual episode frequencies after food.
The review considers diagnostic imaging in Parkinson disease and related syndromes. Clinical phenotype and imaging findings do not supply a dietary intervention or visual episode comparison.

The review describes phenolic studies of Acacia and separately discusses other plant constituents in relation to literature about transient hallucinatory phenomena. That discussion is about a different botanical and chemical exposure. It reports no dried fig or Parkinson visual hallucination-frequency comparison.

The report reviews tracer imaging and clinical use across movement disorders. Its described diagnostic and mechanistic findings do not measure dried fig ingestion paired with visual episode frequency.

The report combines postmortem nigral findings and clinical histories from genetic carriers. The genetic and neuropathological comparison does not identify a dried fig exposure or visual hallucination rate after ingestion.

The authors discuss imaging-guided therapeutic and delivery approaches across neurologic diseases. The narrative and laboratory examples do not supply a dried fig exposure and visual episode-frequency outcome.
The investigation evaluates copy-number variability in a clinical dementia-with-Lewy-bodies sample. Symptoms inform phenotype. No dietary exposure or food-timed visual event response was assessed.

The article reviews psychosis, hallucinations and other nonmotor psychiatric presentations, including disease and medication contributions. The reviewed clinical measures and treatment reports do not test a culinary dried fig exposure.

The paper compares patterns of reduced glucose metabolism and brain atrophy across imaging studies. The endpoint is a group-level anatomical or metabolic pattern. No timed fig or visual episode measure is included.

Investigators followed 273 people with confirmed idiopathic REM sleep behavior disorder across two clinical cohorts. Converting to a defined neurodegenerative syndrome is the principal outcome. The study does not compare visual episode frequency after dried fig intake.

The authors use controlled visual and eye-movement tasks to compare sensory prediction and motor signals in Parkinson disease. The task responses and associated imaging interpretations differ from spontaneous visual hallucination frequency after food.

The paper reviews infusion and other sustained delivery of Parkinson medicines. Apomorphine results and neuropsychiatric concerns are discussed as pharmacologic context. The review does not test a dried fig exposure.

The analysis compares drug studies in Parkinson cognitive impairment, Parkinson dementia and dementia with Lewy bodies. Outcomes include cognition, global impression, behavior and adverse events. The pooled comparisons do not count visual episodes following dried figs.
